context: validation- & commissioning-led · controlled environments · light pharma-style rigor

brief.intro: A laboratory or research facility is a building whose real product is a controlled, contamination-free environment for scientific work — every space is defined by what it must keep in or out: fume extraction, a specific pressure regime, lab gases, or particulate control in a cleanroom. New to this type? It looks like an office or light-industrial building on the outside, but inside it behaves like a light version of a pharmaceutical plant: HVAC is specialist and zoned (pressure cascades between rooms), fume cupboards and lab-gas systems are safety-critical, and nothing is handed over on a fit-out-style snag list alone — spaces are validated and certified (room pressure, air changes, containment) before use. The programme is driven by long-lead specialist equipment (fume cupboards, gas manifolds, cleanroom panels) and by a validation/commissioning tail that cannot be compressed without risking a failed certification.

glossary.plain: a ventilated enclosure that extracts hazardous fumes away from the researcher.
a sequence of rooms held at different, controlled air pressures so air (and contamination) flows the right way — usually from clean to less-clean.
piped gases (nitrogen, compressed air, vacuum, CO2, etc.) supplied to benches from a central manifold.
how many times the room's air volume is replaced per hour — a key HVAC design and validation number for labs.
Installation, Operational and Performance Qualification — staged validation proving equipment is installed correctly, operates correctly, and performs correctly under real conditions.
reverse-osmosis / deionised water — purified water supplied to certain lab benches.
a rating (e.g. an ISO Class) of how few airborne particles a room is certified to contain.

must_get_right: Order fume cupboards, gas manifolds and specialist HVAC equipment against validated lead times, not the general fit-out programme — these are long-lead and safety-critical.
Freeze HVAC and pressure-cascade design before ceilings and walls close — retrofitting a pressure regime after finishes are in is disruptive and slow.
Do not compress the validation/commissioning tail — pressure-cascade balancing and certification are tested conditions, not a snag list, and a failed test means re-balancing, not just a fix.
Coordinate lab-gas and fume-extraction routing with the structural plant-deck design early — heavy rooftop plant and riser space are structural decisions, not late additions.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress; calculated by F9 with total float kept ≥ 0 in the baseline. Validation activities (IQ/OQ/PQ) are modelled as discrete, sequential activities, not folded into a single commissioning bar.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Structure and envelope run a standard 6-day week; specialist HVAC and lab-gas installation often move to a controlled, reduced-dust calendar once cleanroom/containment fit-out starts; validation runs on a calendar built around equipment/room availability rather than a fixed duration.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs long-lead HVAC/fume-cupboard/gas-manifold procurement → structural plant-deck → ductwork/piping rough-in → specialist fit-out → pressure-cascade balancing → IQ/OQ/PQ validation → certification → handover. The building shell is rarely the constraint once weather-tight; validation is the true schedule risk.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: The room-by-room pressure regime and air-change requirements are frozen before ductwork rough-in; specialist equipment (fume cupboards, gas manifolds) is ordered against a fixed design; a single validation authority/consultant is engaged for IQ/OQ/PQ sign-off.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: Specialist HVAC and containment equipment are tracked as milestones and typically drive the network:

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Heavy rooftop/plant-deck equipment needs a crane window and confirmed structural capacity before it is ordered; cleanroom/containment fit-out needs clean, dust-controlled site conditions; validation specialists are a shared, scarce resource across the industry and should be booked well ahead.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: long-lead HVAC/fume-cupboard slippage, a failed pressure-cascade balance or IQ/OQ/PQ test requiring re-work, and late freezing of the room-pressure design forcing ductwork rework. Contingency is held before validation start and before certification.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1–2 to the client; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the specialist-fit-out and validation phases — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
